lines.text: אבי 7 אבל
אבי
For a bullock, Ps. 22, 13 אַבִּירֵי בָשָׁן strong
ones of Bashan, i. e. bulls of Bashan.
50, 13. Metaph. for princes Ps. 68, 31.
b) For a horse, only in Jeremiah, as 8,
2. powerful, potent, noble, Job 24, 22.
34, 20. לֶחֶם אַבִּירִים food of nobles or
princes, i. e. of superior quality, rich
and delicate, Ps. 78, 25; comp. Judg.
5, 25.—אַבִּיר הָרֹעִים chief of the herds-
men 1 Sam. 21, 8.
3. אַבִּיר לֵב stout of heart, i. e. obsti-
nate, wilful, perverse, Is. 46, 12. Comp.
חֲזַק לֵב.
אֲבִירָם (father of altitude) Abiram,
אֲבִישַׁג (father of error) Abishag,
pr. n. of a concubine of David, 1 K. 1, 3.
אֲבִישׁוּעַ (father of welfare) Abishua,
Ezra 7, 5.
אֲבִישׁוּר (father of the wall) Abishur,
אֲבִישַׁי (father of a gift, see שַׁי) Abi-
shai, pr. n. of a son of David’s sister
and one of his chief officers, the brother
of Joab, 1 Sam. 26, 6 sq. 2 Sam. 2, 18.
24; sometimes also written אַבְשַׁי 2 Sam.
אֲבִישָׁלוֹם (father of peace) Abisha-
lom, pr. n. of the father-in-law of Reho-
boam, 1 K. 15, 2. 10. But in 2 Chr. 11,
20. 21, it is written אֲבִשָׁלוֹם.
אֶבְיָתָר (father of abundance, for
אֲבִיָתָר) Abiathar, pr. n. of a son of Ahi-
melech the priest, and a faithful friend
of David, by whom he was made high-
priest along with Zadok, but was de-
posed by Solomon, 1 Sam. 22, 20 sq.
8, 17, see אֲחִימֶלֶךְ.
* אָבַךְ prob. to roll, to roll up or wind,
to entangle. Kindr. roots are בּוּךְ, بَاكَ,
to entangle, to be entangled, intricate,
נָבַךְ to well or boil up, as a fountain, סָבַךְ
to interweave, to braid; also the harsher
הָפַךְ, افك, to turn.—Once
Hithp. to roll itself together, to be
אבל
rolled up, spoken of smoke rolling up-
wards in a dense column; Is. 9, 17
וַיִּתְאַבְּכוּ גֵּאוּת עָשָׁן so that (the thickets)
shall roll upwards as the mounting up
of smoke; comp. Syr. Vulg.—Syr. ܐܬܐܒܟ
is explained by the grammarians as i. q.
to be proud, to walk proudly, perh. pr.
‘to roll oneself forwards,’ in the manner
of a corpulent man.
* I. אָבַל fut. יֶאֱבַל, to mourn, seq.
עַל over any thing Hos. 10, 5. Am. 8, 8.
Arab. Syr. id. The primary idea seems
to be, to be languid, to go with the head
hanging down, as do mourners; comp.
the kindr. roots אָפֵל, אָמַל, also בָּלָה,
נָבֵל, נָפַל, all which are from the bilite-
ral stock bal, fal, and include the idea of
falling, sinking; comp. σφάλλω, fallo,
Germ. fallen, Engl. to fall. It is trans-
ferred also from the dress and manner
of mourners to the voice and to lamen-
tation, see אָבֵל.—Poet. of inanimate
things, Am. 1, 2 אָבְלוּ נְאוֹת־הָרֹעִים the
pastures of the shepherds mourn. Is. 24,
4. 7 אָבַל תִּירוֹשׁ אֻמְלְלָה גָּפֶן the new wine
(i. e. the grapes) mourneth, the vine lan-
guisheth. 33, 9.
Hiph. הֶאֱבִיל to cause to mourn, to
make lament, Ez. 31, 15; of inanimate
things, Lam. 2, 8.
Hithp. pr. to show oneself as mourn-
ing, hence to mourn, i. q. Kal, but chief-
ly in prose, while Kal is more usual in
poetry, Gen. 37, 34. Ex. 33, 4; with אֶל
or עַל of pers. 1 Sam. 15, 35. 2 Sam.
Deriv. אָבֵל I, אֵבֶל.
* II. אָבַל, Arab. أَبَلَ and أَبِلَ to be
moist, wet, sc. with the moisture of
grass; hence Syr. ܐܶܒܳܠܐ grass. Kindr.
is בָּלַל, بَلَّ, to water, יָבַל to flow.
Hence אָבֵל II.
I. אָבֵל adj. (r. אָבַל I,) mourning,
Gen. 37, 35. Lam. 1, 4 דַּרְכֵי צִיּוֹן אֲבֵלוֹת
the ways of Zion are mourning, i. e.
they mourn. Constr. אֲבֶל Ps. 35, 14.
Plur. constr. אֲבֵלֵי Is. 61, 3, with Tsere
impure; comp. Arab. أَبِيل.
II. אָבֵל m. (r. אָבַל II,) prob. a grassy
place, pasture, meadow, Arab. أَبَلٌ fresh

line_status.note: Under the ḥet the print shows a shva pair of dots beside a horizontal bar — ḥaṭef pataḥ (חֲ), as in Reading A; Reading B's qameṣ (חָ) would have a single hooked stroke without the two dots.
Aleph carries ḥaṭef pataḥ (shewa+pataḥ) and bet carries ḥireq, as in B; A's pataḥ+shewa is wrong. No yod printed (defective אֲבִשָׁלוֹם).
The Arabic initial alif is printed bare (افك) with no hamza above it; Reading B's أ is not in the print. Hebrew points, Hebrew/Arabic order, and English match in both.
Under the pe of the first root the print shows two dots (tsere, אָפֵל), not a single patah stroke; contrast with the single patah visible under the mem of אָמַל.
Under the bet of the first word the print shows two side-by-side dots (tsere), not a single horizontal stroke (patah) as under the pe of נָפַל; so נָבֵל, matching Gesenius's lemma form.

The Syriac word carries only two vowel marks in print: one over the initial alaph and one over the beth; the lamadh has no point at all. Reading A adds a zqapha over the lamadh that is not printed; Reading B leaves the beth unpointed and puts the zqapha on the lamadh, which is also not what is printed. Everything else on the line (grass; hence Syr. … grass. Kindr.) agrees.
A curled tanwīn ḍamm (ٌ) is clearly printed above the final lām of the Arabic word; Reading A drops it. Hamza+fatḥa on alif and fatḥa on bā are as both readings give.
